Monomials. A monomial is a single term consisting of a constant coefficient multiplied by a variable raised to a non-negative integer power. Monomials are the building blocks of polynomials and the simplest algebraic functions, including constants, linear terms, and pure powers of x.

The general form is f of x equals a times x to the n, where a is a nonzero constant and n is a non-negative integer. The degree of a monomial is the exponent n, and a is the coefficient. A degree zero monomial is just a constant. Degree one is a linear term ax. Degree two is quadratic. Higher degrees are certainly possible. Monomials are the individual terms in a polynomial—a polynomial with exactly one term is a monomial, two terms is a binomial, three is a trinomial. All monomials are continuous, differentiable, and defined for all real x, with smooth curves as their graphs. The derivative of a times x to the n is n times a times x to the n minus one, which is itself a monomial, or zero if n equals zero. This simple structure makes monomials the entry point to understanding polynomial functions.
